report: Conclusion: the claim is **overstated**. CLA is not a reliable or clinically meaningful way to reduce abdominal fat. The best direct support is a small 4-week RCT in abdominally obese men with metabolic-syndrome features: CLA reduced sagittal abdominal diameter, but did **not** reduce overall obesity or improve cardiovascular risk factors, limiting generalizability (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/11477497/). Broader evidence is weak: a 2007 human meta-analysis found only a small average fat-mass effect—about 0.05 kg/week at ~3.2 g/day—and not specifically abdominal/visceral fat (https://ajcn.nutrition.org/article/S0002-9165(23)28055-7/fulltext). A 2023 systematic review/dose–response meta-analysis reported small average improvements, but **high-quality studies failed to confirm body-fat-lowering effects**, suggesting bias or inconsistency in positive findings (https://www.cambridge.org/core/journals/british-journal-of-nutrition/article/effects-of-conjugated-linoleic-acid-supplementation-on-anthropometrics-and-body-composition-indices-in-adults-a-systematic-review-and-doseresponse-metaanalysis/A3F12F07BB3118D4F757D901C6E1E366). Safety is also not neutral: in type 2 diabetes patients, CLA adversely affected insulin and glucose metabolism (https://pubmed.ncbi.nlm.nih.gov/15447895/). Overall, any abdominal-fat effect is likely small, short-term, population-specific, and outweighed by uncertain quality and possible metabolic harms; diet, exercise, sleep, and clinically supervised weight management remain better-supported.
